question: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency room because of confusion. His wife says he has been urinating more frequently than usual for the past 3 days. He has not had fever or dysuria. He has bipolar disorder, for which he takes lithium. His pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 14/min. He is lethargic and oriented only to person. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and increased capillary refill time. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium concentration of 158 mEq/L and an antidiuretic hormone (ADH) concentration of 8 pg/mL (N = 1–5). Which of the following is the most likely site of dysfunction in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Lithium intake -> nephrogenic diabetes insipidus -> increased urine output -> dehydration -> hypernatremia -> confusion -> 90%
CHAIN: Lithium intake -> inhibition of ADH action -> decreased water reabsorption in the collecting duct -> increased urine output -> dehydration -> hypernatremia -> confusion -> 85%
enhanced_information: In this case, the most likely site of dysfunction in the patient is the collecting duct due to lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. This leads to decreased water reabsorption, increased urine output, dehydration, hypernatremia, and subsequent confusion. The evidence paths support the relationship between lithium and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, as well as the complications of hypernatremia leading to confusion.
analysis: The patient's presentation with lithium use, polyuria, hypernatremia, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus suggests dysfunction at the collecting duct level. Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus impairs water reabsorption at the collecting duct, leading to the observed symptoms.
